title: Indian-American Grandmother Granted Bail After ICE Detained Her Despite Dismissed Case
excerpt: Venkata Vasamsetty, a green card holder for 13 years with no criminal record, was detained by ICE during a routine check-in months after an immigration judge dismissed removal proceedings against her.
body:
• Venkata Vasamsetty, 60, was detained by ICE on Aug. 11 during a routine check-in despite an immigration judge dismissing her removal case in May
  • The green card holder since 2013 was flagged for staying in India longer than six months, a trip extended by COVID-19 hospitalization while caring for dying parents
  • An immigration judge granted $7,500 bail, finding DHS had not proven she was a flight risk, citing her 27-year ties to the U.S.
  • Her case has drawn attention from members of Congress and highlights broader concerns about ICE enforcement against lawful permanent residents

An Indian-American grandmother who has held a green card for 13 years and lived in the United States for 27 years has been granted bail after Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained her during a routine check-in, months after an immigration judge dismissed removal proceedings against her.

Venkata Narsamamba Vasamsetty, 60, was taken into custody on Aug. 11 when she reported to ICE's Charlotte, North Carolina, office for a scheduled check-in. She was transported to Georgia's Irwin County Detention Center and told she would be processed for deportation because she did not possess a valid green card, according to her attorneys.

A Trip Extended by COVID

The case traces back to 2022, when Vasamsetty traveled to India to care for her elderly and critically ill parents. During her stay, she contracted COVID-19 and was hospitalized for nearly two weeks, suffering additional complications that prevented her from traveling. Her trip, originally planned for less than six months, stretched to about seven months — past the 180-day threshold that can trigger questions about whether a permanent resident has abandoned their U.S. residency.

The Department of Homeland Security initiated removal proceedings, arguing Vasamsetty's extended absence demonstrated she had abandoned her permanent resident status. Her attorneys disputed this, pointing to evidence that she maintained substantial ties to the United States throughout her trip.

"She wasn't packing up her life in the United States. She wasn't moving back to India. She wasn't leaving with the intention of giving up her green card. At the time she left, she was literally in the process of buying a home in North Carolina."

— Zoe Wilson, Immigration Attorney

Vasamsetty returned to the United States through Raleigh-Durham International Airport in February 2023. She had completed the purchase of a new home in North Carolina during her time abroad — a fact her lawyers said demonstrated her intent to remain in the country.

Case Dismissed, Then Detained

On May 19, an immigration judge terminated the government's removal case after DHS failed to meet a court-imposed deadline to submit evidence supporting its claims. Despite the dismissal, Vasamsetty continued attending her scheduled ICE check-ins.

When she appeared at the Charlotte office on Aug. 11, she was arrested. Her legal team filed an emergency habeas corpus petition on Aug. 13, and a federal judge ordered immigration authorities to explain the legal basis for her detention.

Representative Deborah Ross of North Carolina called the detention unlawful, saying Vasamsetty "is being denied food and insulin, and shouldn't even be in custody to begin with."

Bail Granted at $7,500

During a bond hearing, DHS attorney Abby Cannon said Vasamsetty was not a danger to the community but posed a "significant flight risk," citing her travel history between the United States and India. DHS argued she spent only 61 days in the U.S. in 2019, 96 days in 2021, and 67 days in 2022. Vasamsetty's family disputed those travel dates.

Her attorney Helen Parsonage argued that Vasamsetty's trips to India were primarily to care for her aging parents, including her father before his death. Parsonage noted that Vasamsetty never missed an immigration court appearance or ICE check-in.

Judge Chad Bayse found that DHS had not met its burden of proving Vasamsetty would flee. He cited her long-standing ties to the United States, including her husband, two U.S.-citizen daughters, grandchildren, a home, tax returns dating to at least 2012, and her work as an elementary school substitute teacher serving special-needs students. However, he set bail at $7,500 rather than the minimum, noting some flight risk due to her international travel history.

What Comes Next

Vasamsetty must appear at all future court dates, comply with court orders, and avoid arrests. DHS has until Sept. 24 to appeal the bond decision. Her attorneys said she has diabetes and requires ongoing medical care and glucose monitoring.

Her case comes amid an ongoing national debate over ICE enforcement practices. Vasamsetty's attorney told reporters the legal fight is far from over, with her team preparing to challenge any further attempts to remove her from the country she has called home for nearly three decades.
nri_angle: The detention of a longtime green card holder over a COVID-extended trip to care for dying parents has alarmed Indian-American communities concerned about the security of their immigration status.
author: Diaspora Desk
